newsitem.title: CANADA: Minister calls for vote on Canadian plan.
newsitem.headline: Minister calls for vote on Canadian plan.

text.p: Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said on Friday he wanted the employees of troubled Canadian Airlines Corp to be able to vote on a restructuring plan proposed by the company.

"I completely agree that the employees of Canadian should have the right to vote on their future and on the restructuring program that has been proposed by Mr. (Kevin) Benson, the (chief executive) of Canadian Airlines," Anderson told parliament under questioning from opposition deputies.
Anderson repeated that his government did not intend to bail out Canadian by providing direct cash assistance.

"We want to make sure that plan has a fair chance and I know it's difficult for the employees, but we want them to be able to vote on that plan...a government bailout does not appear to be a viable option," he said.
Last week Canadian said it would go out of business unless it could enact a tough restructuring program involving employee wage rollbacks, route changes and reduced fees to 33 percent owner AMR Corp.

But Canadian's biggest union, the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists, repeated on Friday that it would not support an employee vote on Canadian's life-support plan, which includes a call for a 10 percent wage cut for all workers.
"There's no movement on that," said IAM spokesman Neville Hamilton. "We have a collective agreement in place and we're showing some leadership on the issue and that's it."
Hamilton said a mechanism existed for the members to review the collective agreement, but that there had been no indication of plans to use it.
"(The members) are taking the leadership that the union is providing on this issue and we're hanging tough," he said.

Union officials for IAM and Canadian's 3,700 workers who belong to the Canadian Auto Workers union, rejected the company's wage cut demands and called on the government for a bailout and changes to air industry regulations.
Anderson told reporters after speaking in parliament that he had not checked to see if the government could force the unions to hold a vote.
"I do not know whether it is possible for a minister to force a vote," he said.

Anderson said: "I am relying at this point on the obvious fairness of the request that is being made to the machinists and the CAW. It does not seem fair to allow people's jobs to be put in jeopardy without them having the opportunity of deciding whether they wish or wish not to proceed with the plan proposed by the company."
When told the union executives had rejected a vote, Anderson suggested it was not their decision to make.

"I think that's a position which under the circumstances is inappropriate because I believe that it is not the union executive who will lose their jobs if indeed the company's plan fails and things get worse.
"It is of course the employees of Canadian International. They may vote against the plan. That is certainly their right and I am not attempting to influence them on that point," Anderson said.
